content: Hymenolepis infection, also known as hymenolepiasis, is caused by infestation with one of two species of tapeworm: Hymenolepis nana or Hymenolepis diminuta. Among these, Hymenolepis nana infections are significantly more common in humans. This is because, in addition to being transmitted by insects, H. nana can also spread directly from person to person through eggs present in feces. Humans and other animals become infected when they ingest material contaminated by insects, either intentionally or unintentionally. In individuals who are infected, the entire life cycle of the worm can be completed within the intestines, allowing the infection to persist for years. Most individuals infected with Hymenolepis do not exhibit any symptoms. However, those who do may experience nausea, weakness, loss of appetite, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. In young children, particularly those with heavy infections, symptoms may include headaches, an itchy anal region, or difficulty sleeping. Occasionally, the infection may be misdiagnosed as a pinworm infection. Contrary to popular belief, tapeworm infections generally do not cause weight loss, and individuals cannot feel the presence of the tapeworm inside their body. The diagnosis of hymenolepiasis is confirmed through stool examination for eggs and parasites. The use of concentration techniques and repeated stool examinations increases the likelihood of detecting light infections. The eggs and proglottids (segments of the tapeworm) of H. nana are smaller than those of H. diminuta. The proglottids of both species are relatively wide and contain three testes. Treatment involves the administration of a prescription medication called praziquantel. This drug works by causing the tapeworm to dissolve within the intestines. Praziquantel is generally well-tolerated, but in some cases, more than one course of treatment may be required.
